newsitem.title: CANADA: FOCUS-Abitibi-Price, Stone-Consolidated agree to merge.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Abitibi-Price, Stone-Consolidated agree to merge.

text.p: Abitibi-Price Inc., the world's largest newsprint maker, and Stone-Consolidated Corp. said on Friday they agreed to merge in a stock swap transaction.

Under the agreement, each common share of Toronto-based Abitibi-Price will be exchanged for one common share of the merged company, Abitibi-Consolidated Inc. Each common share of Stone-Consolidated, headquartered in Montreal, will be exchanged for 1.0062 common shares of Abitibi-Consolidated.

Abitibi-Consolidated would be the world's biggest newsprint maker by a margin of almost two-to-one, with annual newsprint production of more than 3.2 million metric tons. It would have 18 paper mills, including 14 in Canada, three in the United States and one in Britain.
The company would also have seven wholly owned or affiliated sawmills in Canada.

The companies said Abitibi-Price Chairman and Chief Executive Ronald Oberlander would be operating chairman of Abitibi-Consolidated. Stone-Consolidated President and Chief Executive James Doughan would be president and chief executive of the merged company.

Stone Container Corp., of Chicago, which owns 46.6 percent of Stone Consolidated, agreed to vote for the transaction. After the merger it would hold about 25 percent of Abitibi-Consolidated, the companies said. The transaction was expected to close in the second quarter.

The merged company would have a market capitalization of about C$4.1 billion ($3.1 billion) and annual revenues of about C$4.9 billion ($3.6 billion). The companies said they identified cost savings of more than C$100 million ($74 million) yearly from the merger.

"This merger of equals will create a far stronger company from both an operating and financial perspective and will provide a strong platform from which to launch our future growth," Oberlander said in a statement.
The companies said they believed the merger would boost earnings for the merged company in the first 12 months after the closing.
Analysts said the merged company would be much more dominant in the newsprint market.

"When they take production downtime, that will have an effect on the market, and when they announce a price increase, people will sit up and take notice," said Jim Rowland, publisher of the Canadian Paper Analyst, an industry newsletter.

Until the late 1980s, Toronto's wealthy Reichmann family held a majority interest in Abitibi-Price, but sold the stake to focus on its then troubled real estate holdings. Abitibi-Price is now widely held, although analysts said a Boston-based hedge fund, Tiger Management, might be its largest shareholder with an 11 percent stake.

Stone Container acquired Stone-Consolidated in the late 1980s from Power Corp of Canada, a Montreal-based financial and industrial holding company. Analysts said Roger Stone, chairman, president and chief executive of Stone Container, might eventually want to sell his 25 percent stake in the new merged company in keeping with his strategy to focus on his company's core packaging business.

The merger between Abitibi-Price and Stone-Consolidated comes with North American newsprint prices at their lowest level in the current price cycle. Many analysts expect newsprint to rebound from its current level of $500 a metric ton by the second half of this year.

Over the past year, most Canadian newsprint makers have cut back production to address inventory imbalances caused by weak demand for newsprint in North America and growing competition from overseas producers. Before the merger announcement, Abitibi-Price had been seeking to sell its newsprint mill in Thunder Bay, Ontario, and at least one other in Quebec.

Abitibi-Price closed up C5 cents to C$22.30 on the Toronto Stock Exchange on Friday and was unchanged at $16.50 on the New York Stock Exchange. Stone-Consolidated rose C$1.35 to C$22.25 in Toronto, while Stone Container fell 12.5 cents to $12.75 in New York.
